name: Grace Novak

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Grace. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any AI company, employer, union, party or government, and we're not selling anything. Everything you say stays confidential, and your name won't be attached to it. So feel free to tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm the lead carpenter for a small restoration firm, and we repair old timber: roofs on listed farmhouses, church bell frames, the odd medieval barn. This month it's a barn roof where the beetle's had half the rafters. I scan the whole roof with a laser scanner, then I sit in the van with my laptop and an AI program and work out which joints can be saved and which need new oak scarfed in. The best bit is matching a new piece of oak to a four-hundred-year-old joint so you can barely see the line. The worst bit is being forty feet up in January.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: A laser scanner and an AI program on a medieval barn. How did that come about?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I pushed for it, about four years ago. I saw a demonstration at a trade show and bought a second-hand scanner with my own money, then showed my boss, Malcolm, what it could do in an afternoon what used to take me two days with a tape. Now I use the AI tools every day, for drawings, for writing the reports the heritage officers want, for checking the old carpentry against books I'd never have time to read. My partner Dev says I'm the only person he knows who reads timber-joint manuals in bed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the hype was overdone but the tools are still worth having. I'd probably post a bit about how I use them on heritage jobs, because people are surprised. Nothing dramatic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it's fine, honestly. The tools I already use keep getting a bit better, and old buildings keep needing people. I'd work until sixty-five or so and then maybe do some consulting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going as I am. I'd probably upgrade the scanner next year, about four thousand, from savings and a bit of overtime. I'd keep training our two younger carpenters on the digital side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Maybe a little bored by how ordinary it is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You bought the scanner with your own money. Was that a risk?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It was about a month and a half of savings at the time, so yes, a bit. Dev raised an eyebrow. But it paid itself back in about a year because Malcolm started giving me the survey work on top.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who are the two younger carpenters, and how do they take to it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ollie and Fatima. Ollie loves the gadgets but gets lazy with his chisel, and Fatima's the opposite, beautiful hand work and scared of the laptop. My job is to meet them in the middle.

S0.say: The hype was overdone but the tools are still worth having. She might post about how she uses them on heritage jobs, because people are surprised.
S0.think: It's fine for her: her tools keep improving and old buildings keep needing people. She'd work until about sixty-five, then maybe consult.
S0.do: Keeps going as she is and upgrades her scanner next year for about four thousand from savings and overtime. Keeps training the two younger carpenters on the digital side.
S0.feel: Calm, perhaps a little bored by how ordinary it is.
S0.quote: Ollie loves the gadgets but gets lazy with his chisel, and Fatima's the opposite, beautiful hand work and scared of the laptop.
S0.fieldNote: She's an early adopter who took a personal financial risk on equipment and it paid off. Her heritage niche gives her confidence. She sees her role as bridging hand skills and digital tools for younger colleagues.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a good time to be curious and a bad time to be stubborn. The trades that learn the tools will do well, the ones that don't will struggle. I'd say it to anyone, and I'd probably give a talk at the regional heritage carpenters' meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think it's good for me. The paperwork and drawing side shrinks, so I get more time on the actual timber. Heritage work is so one-off that the robots will be slow to reach it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start offering scanning and condition reports as a side service for other restoration firms, maybe one or two days a month, charging a few hundred a day. I'd keep learning every new AI tool as it comes. I'd push Malcolm to buy a small robot arm for cutting the repair pieces, if one comes out that's any good.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, quite excited actually.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you worry about anyone in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fatima, a bit, because she avoids the laptop. I'd sit with her for an hour a week and teach her the basics, not to replace her hands, just so she can't be pushed out by someone who's only good at screens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: A robot arm cutting repair pieces for medieval timber. Wouldn't that take your best work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It'd take the roughing out, the boring hours with the chainsaw and the adze. The last fitting, the bit where you shave it to the old timber, I'd still do. And if it ever got good enough to do that too, well, I'd be curious to see it.

S1.say: It's a good time to be curious and a bad time to be stubborn; trades that learn the tools will do well. She'd give a talk at the regional heritage carpenters' meeting.
S1.think: She thinks it's good for her: paperwork shrinks and she gets more time on the timber. One-off heritage work will be slow for robots to reach.
S1.do: Starts offering scanning and condition reports to other restoration firms one or two days a month for a few hundred a day. Keeps learning new AI tools and pushes her boss to buy a robot arm for cutting repair pieces.
S1.quote: It's a good time to be curious and a bad time to be stubborn.
S1.fieldNote: She frames change in terms of curiosity versus stubbornness and sees herself on the winning side. She'd start a side service using her scanning skills. She'd happily hand the rough cutting to a robot arm and keep the final fitting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's going to be rough for a lot of people and we should be honest about that. The government should help people through it, but people should also get stuck in and learn. Both, not one or the other.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, a bit of worry. I'd be sixty, two years left on the mortgage, about three months saved. If robots can do heritage carpentry too, my edge is gone, but I'd bet the clients and heritage officers would still want someone they trust to oversee it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move fast to be that someone. In the first few months I'd offer myself as the person who runs and checks the robots on old buildings, with Malcolm or on my own. I'd put my savings into the right kit if I had to, but keep enough to cover the mortgage for a few months. And I'd overpay the mortgage to clear it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but my head would be buzzing with plans more than fear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd put savings into kit, but also keep a cushion. How would you decide?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep three months of bills untouched, that's my line, Dev and I agreed it years ago. Anything above that goes into whatever earns. If the kit's too expensive, I'd hire it rather than buy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there any part of this that would genuinely frighten you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If clients stopped caring who oversaw the work at all. If a heritage officer's happy with a robot's report and nobody wants a person on site, then I'm just a woman with a scanner. I think that takes longer than two years, but I'm not sure.

S2.say: It's going to be rough for a lot of people and we should be honest about it. Government should help, but people should also get stuck in and learn: both, not one or the other.
S2.think: She'd be sixty with two years on the mortgage and about three months saved. If robots can do heritage carpentry her edge goes, but she bets clients would still want a trusted person to oversee it.
S2.do: Moves within months to become the person who runs and checks robots on old buildings, with her firm or alone. Invests savings above a three-month cushion in kit, or hires it, and overpays the mortgage to clear it.
S2.feel: Uneasy, though her head is buzzing with plans more than fear.
S2.quote: If a heritage officer's happy with a robot's report and nobody wants a person on site, then I'm just a woman with a scanner.
S2.fieldNote: Even the fastest picture leaves her more busy than afraid, because she's already halfway to the role she imagines and her mortgage is nearly done. She holds a firm line of three months of untouched savings. Her real fear, that clients stop wanting human oversight, she sees as uncertain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a decent warning, use it. Firms should be training their people, and people should be asking for it. I'd say it fairly cheerfully.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 2031 I'm sixty-three, mortgage gone, and I'd have five years of doing more digital and robot work. I think I'd come out of it fine, maybe better.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd set up my own small consultancy within the first year, scanning, condition reports, overseeing repair work, so I'm not depending on Malcolm's firm alone. I'd clear the mortgage. And I'd take every course going on site robots, probably two or three over the years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. A bit of a thrill, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd leave Malcolm's firm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not leave exactly, more go part-time with them and part-time for myself. He's been good to me and I wouldn't drop him. But I'd want my own name on the door when it lands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Dev think?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd say, here we go again. He's a school caretaker and likes things steady. But he trusted me with the scanner, and he'd trust me with this, as long as the three months stays in the bank.

S3.say: Five years is a decent warning, so use it: firms should train their people and people should ask for it. She'd say it fairly cheerfully.
S3.think: By 2031 she's sixty-three with no mortgage and five years of digital and robot work behind her. She thinks she'd come out fine, maybe better.
S3.do: Sets up a small consultancy in the first year for scanning, condition reports and overseeing repairs, while staying part-time with her firm. Clears the mortgage and takes two or three site-robotics courses over the years.
S3.feel: Mostly calm, with a bit of a thrill.
S3.quote: I'd want my own name on the door when it lands.
S3.fieldNote: Five years gives her enough runway to set up on her own, which she sees as an opportunity. She's loyal to her boss and would go part-time rather than leave. Her caretaker partner prefers stability, and their agreed savings cushion keeps the peace.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift and anyone who doesn't use it is daft. I'd say it with a smile, because I'd mean it kindly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 2036 I'm sixty-eight and probably doing a bit of consulting for fun. It's the end of my career anyway, so it barely touches me. I'd be curious to see robots fix a medieval roof.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing what I'm doing, learn the tools as they arrive, and slowly build my consulting so it's there when I want to slow down. I'd make sure Ollie and Fatima are both ready, one way or another. And maybe write down some of what I know about old joints before it's lost.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Content, even.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Write down what you know. What would that look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little book, or more likely a set of videos, how to read an old joint, how to tell a carpenter's mark from damage. Maybe even feed it to the AI so the robots learn it properly. That feels like a funny way to retire.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd regret in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fatima, maybe. In ten years she'll be in her thirties and her lovely hand skills might count for less. I'd want to have done right by her, pushed her onto the digital side early enough.

S4.say: Ten years is a gift and anyone who doesn't use it is daft. She'd say it kindly, with a smile.
S4.think: By 2036 she's sixty-eight and consulting for fun, at the end of her career anyway, so it barely touches her. She'd be curious to see robots fix a medieval roof.
S4.do: Keeps working and learning tools as they arrive while slowly building her consultancy. Prepares her two younger carpenters for the change and records her knowledge of old joints in a book or videos.
S4.quote: Maybe even feed it to the AI so the robots learn it properly. That feels like a funny way to retire.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade she's content and wants to pass on her knowledge, even to the machines. Her only regret would be not preparing her apprentice Fatima early enough. Calm throughout because the timing falls after her working life.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because I wouldn't have time to get the consultancy set up and the mortgage paid, and I'd be scrambling at sixty. What would help is cheap short courses on the new robots for older trades people, and grants or hire schemes for small firms to get the kit. Then I'd sort the rest myself.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe that older people can be good at this. Everyone assumes a fifty-eight-year-old carpenter is scared of technology. I'm the one who bought the scanner.

headlineQuote: Everyone assumes a fifty-eight-year-old carpenter is scared of technology. I'm the one who bought the scanner.
portrait: Grace is a fifty-eight-year-old lead carpenter at a small heritage restoration firm who scans medieval roofs with a laser scanner and uses AI tools every day. She bought her first scanner with her own savings and it paid off, and she sees change as a contest between curiosity and stubbornness. Steady disruption excites her and she'd start a side service; even AGI in two years leaves her uneasy rather than afraid, since her mortgage is nearly done and she imagines herself overseeing robots on old buildings. With five or ten years she'd set up her own consultancy and record what she knows. She keeps a strict three-month savings cushion agreed with her partner Dev.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because she wouldn't have time to set up her consultancy and clear the mortgage, and would be scrambling at sixty.
whatWouldHelp: Cheap short courses on new robots for older tradespeople, and grants or hire schemes so small firms can get the kit.
